newsitem.title: USA: Dollar edges up in early U.S. trading.
newsitem.headline: Dollar edges up in early U.S. trading.

text.p: The dollar climbed Monday after the Group of Seven leading industrial nations' statement on Sunday citing concerns about the currency's strength failed to deter traders who saw it as a green light to buy the dollar.
The dollar popped above 127 Japanese yen in Asian trading but later backed off and stood at 126.60 yen in early New York trading, up from 126.25 late in New York on Friday.
The dollar also rose against the German mark, touching 1.7395 marks, the highest since February 1994, but gave much of the gains back and stood at 1.7280, up from 1.7275 at Friday's New York close.
"Nobody has said this is overdone and we're going to intervene. I think that is what the market was fearing," said Richard Vullo, of Bayerische Hypotheken und Weschelsbank.

The G7 ministers ended their meeting in Washington Sunday with a statement warning that the dollar had risen enough, though they did not specify any steps to bring it down. And there were no signs of central banks stepping in to sell dollars in world currency markets on Monday, traders said.

"Jawboning isn't enough, only intervention will stop it in the short-term," said one trader at a leading U.S. bank. "And there is a big enough question mark over possible intervention to keep the dollar bulls happy."

G7 finance officials and central bankers said in their statement Sunday that excessive volatility in currency markets was undesirable and stressed the need to avoid exchange rates that could lead to renewed large trade imbalances.
The statement was bereft of specific references to current dollar levels and traders said there was little change in tone from the last G7 meeting in February.

"The only thing really new (was that) they don't want to see the trade balance going out of whack," said Diego Giurleo, a vice president at Royal Bank of Canada. "Of course, that was an indirect reference to dollar-yen."

The dollar rose about 40 percent against the yen last year, and has continued to climb, though more gradually, since the G7's statement in February. The weaker yen makes Japanese exports more competitive in world markets and could fuel a jump in Japan's big trade surplus with the United States.
In addition to the lack of specific pledges or action to bring the dollar down, several remarks by G7 officials after the meeting lent additional support to the dollar, traders said.
They noted that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin had steered clear of calling for an end to the dollar's rise, saying the G7 statement spoke for itself.

But German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer knocked some wind from the dollar's sails, telling reporters that the United States was very interested in having a "strong dollar, but not a stronger one."
Bank of England Governor Eddie George said the G7 believed that the currency market was in "pretty good shape" and saw no reason to draw up an action plan to bring it back into line.
The British pound was little changed at $1.6240 from $1.6235.
The dollar rose to 1.4695 Swiss francs from 1.4690 and to Canadian $1.3980 from C$1.3975.
